Decrypt\u2019s reporting added that the firm operated more than 9,000 Bitcoin ATM locations across North America before the closure. The bankruptcy filing landed in Texas federal court, and the company said the process is intended to support an orderly wind-down of operations and a sale of the company\u2019s assets.\n\nCEO Alex Holmes blamed an increasingly hostile regulatory environment for the collapse. In Decrypt\u2019s account, Holmes said the regulatory framework for Bitcoin ATM operators has \u201cshifted significantly,\u201d leaving the company\u2019s business model unsustainable. Holmes also said operators have faced increasing litigation and regulatory enforcement, which materially affected Bitcoin Depot\u2019s business and financial position. The company posted a $9.5 million net loss in the quarter, compared with $12.2 million in net income a year earlier. Investor confidence had also collapsed: Decrypt said the stock had dropped 79.48% over the prior six months as regulatory uncertainty intensified and the business weakened. Earlier reports also indicated that the company had been warning about bankruptcy risk as ATM revenue fell and legal pressure increased.\n\nBitcoin Depot\u2019s troubles were not isolated to revenue. Decrypt said the company overhauled leadership in March 2026, appointing Holmes as CEO after Connecticut suspended its money transmission license. A month later, the company disclosed that hackers had breached its IT systems and stolen $3.7 million from its crypto wallets. The firm was also dealing with ongoing legal battles involving an $18.5 million award dispute tied to its Canadian subsidiary. Those compounding pressures helped push the operator toward court-supervised restructuring.\n\nThe filing lands in a broader period of strain for the Bitcoin ATM sector. Decrypt noted that Tennessee became the second state to outlaw Bitcoin ATMs after Indiana in April, while Canadian authorities have also proposed restrictions. The company\u2019s collapse underscores how quickly a business built on consumer access to cash-to-Bitcoin kiosks can be squeezed by tightening rules, enforcement action, and declining transaction economics. What once looked like a high-growth retail gateway for Bitcoin adoption is now colliding with a much harsher compliance and liability environment.\n\nCoinDesk\u2019s headline framed the event as a bankruptcy filing by the company that was once North America\u2019s largest bitcoin ATM operator. Decrypt\u2019s more detailed coverage made clear how severe the unwind has become: a full shutdown of more than 9,000 machines, a Chapter 11 process in Texas, planned Canadian proceedings, a sharp revenue drop, a quarterly loss after prior profitability, a major stock decline, and additional legal and security setbacks. Together, the two reports show a single major crypto business event centered on Bitcoin infrastructure, regulation, and the viability of the cash-to-crypto ATM model in 2026."
}

# Bitcoin Depot files for Chapter 11 after 49.2% revenue drop

Bitcoin Depot has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection after a brutal collapse in operating performance, with Q1 2026 revenue down 49.2% year over year. The company said it is starting an orderly wind-down and sale process after shutting down a network that once covered more than 9,000 bitcoin ATM locations across North America.

The market signal was already there before the filing hit. Bitcoin Depot shares had fallen 79.48% over the past six months, and the company swung to a $9.5 million net loss from $12.2 million in net income a year earlier. That kind of reversal usually tells traders the balance sheet problem is no longer theoretical.

This is not a one-day shock. It looks like a business model that ran out of room under heavier regulation and weaker economics.

## Chapter 11 bankruptcy: What It Means for Bitcoin Depot

According to [CoinDesk](https://www.coindesk.com/markets/2026/05/18/bitcoin-depot-once-north-america-s-largest-bitcoin-atm-operator-files-for-bankruptcy), Bitcoin Depot filed in Texas federal court and framed the process as a controlled wind-down tied to a sale of the company or its assets. That matters because Chapter 11 bankruptcy does not always mean an immediate liquidation, but it does mean management has lost confidence in the current structure.

The filing also shows how fast compliance pressure can turn a consumer-facing crypto business into a restructuring case. In a more detailed report, [Decrypt said](https://decrypt.co/368146/crypto-atm-operator-bitcoin-depot-files-for-chapter-11-bankruptcy) the company blamed stricter transaction limits, bans or restrictions in some jurisdictions, and rising enforcement and litigation costs for making the model unsustainable.

[CHART_PLACEHOLDER]

### Compliance costs broke the operating model

CEO Alex Holmes pointed directly at regulation as the core issue. The business was built around cash-to-Bitcoin access, but that model gets squeezed quickly when every new transaction limit reduces throughput and every new rule adds cost.

The pressure was not coming from one market alone. The company also expects separate restructuring proceedings in Canada, which shows the problem was broader than a single U.S. state action.

- New transaction limits reduced revenue per kiosk.
- State bans and restrictions cut geographic reach.
- Litigation and enforcement raised fixed costs at the worst possible time.

### A 9,000-machine shutdown changes the Bitcoin ATM sector

The shutdown of more than 9,000 machines is the real signal for the Bitcoin ATM sector. Scale was once Bitcoin Depot's edge, but scale also magnifies overhead when traffic slows and compliance gets tougher.

That network size made Bitcoin Depot a visible retail access point for casual bitcoin buyers. With the machines offline, the sector loses one of its largest operators, and smaller players now face a harder question about whether volume can still cover compliance, security, and legal risk.

Another [Decrypt report detail](https://decrypt.co/368146/crypto-atm-operator-bitcoin-depot-files-for-chapter-11-bankruptcy) adds to that pressure. The company disclosed a $3.7 million theft from its crypto wallets after an IT systems breach, which means operational risk was rising at the same time revenue was falling.

## Key numbers Bitcoin ATM sector traders should watch now

The bankruptcy headline matters, but the numbers underneath it matter more for the Bitcoin ATM sector. Traders and investors should track whether this was a company-specific blowup or the start of a wider repricing across listed crypto access businesses and adjacent payment infrastructure.

[CHART_PLACEHOLDER]

### 49.2% revenue decline is the first signal

A 49.2% year-over-year revenue drop is not a mild slowdown. It suggests either transaction demand fell sharply, unit economics deteriorated, or both happened at once. When a company moves from positive earnings to a $9.5 million net loss in a year, recovery usually requires more than cost cuts.

For market participants, that figure is the cleanest measure of stress. If peers begin posting similar declines, the Bitcoin ATM sector may be entering a structural contraction rather than a temporary reset.

### 79.48% stock collapse shows where confidence broke

The six-month stock decline of 79.48% shows equity investors were pricing in failure before the court filing arrived. That kind of move usually reflects fear of dilution, asset sales under pressure, and a low chance that the existing business can stabilize without a major reset.

The next step is to watch whether the bankruptcy process attracts credible buyers or just confirms that the installed network has less value than previously assumed.

- Look for: updates on asset sale interest and restructuring terms.
- Look for: new state restrictions that could pressure other ATM operators.
- Look for: Canadian court filings, wallet security fallout, and any copycat stress at peers.

## Conclusion

Bitcoin Depot has become the clearest warning sign in the Bitcoin ATM business, with a Chapter 11 filing following a 49.2% revenue decline and a full network shutdown.

Near term, the structure is simple. If this remains an isolated failure, the fallout stays contained. If similar operators start posting the same revenue damage, the sector likely trades lower and funding gets tighter.

Watch the sale process, state-level regulation, and any signs that peers are losing volume at the same pace. Bitcoin Depot may be the first large casualty here, but traders should assume it will not be the last unless the data improves fast.

## FAQs

**1. Why did Bitcoin Depot file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy happen?**

Bitcoin Depot said its business became unsustainable as compliance rules tightened and transaction limits increased. The company also faced bans or restrictions in some jurisdictions, plus rising litigation and enforcement costs. Those pressures hit while revenue was already weakening. By the time the filing arrived, the company had moved from profit to loss and shut down its machine network.

**2. Is this the start of a bigger trend?**

It could be, but one filing is not enough to confirm a sector-wide collapse. What makes this event important is Bitcoin Depot's size and its previous leadership position in North America. If other operators report similar revenue declines, security incidents, or regulatory setbacks, the market will likely treat this as the start of a broader reset in crypto ATM economics.

**3. What numbers should traders watch now?**

The first number is the 49.2% revenue decline because it shows how severe the business slowdown became. The second is the 79.48% stock drop, which signals how much confidence had already broken before bankruptcy. Traders should also track any recovery values from the asset sale process. If those numbers disappoint, it will pressure valuations across related names.

**4. How does this affect Bitcoin and the wider market?**

The direct effect on Bitcoin price may be limited because Bitcoin Depot was an access channel, not a protocol-level player. The bigger impact is on retail on-ramp infrastructure and on public market sentiment around compliance-heavy crypto businesses. It could also shift more users toward exchanges and other digital onboarding options. That would weaken the investment case for physical kiosk networks.

**5. What is the historical context for this move?**

Bitcoin ATMs grew during earlier adoption waves because they offered simple cash access to bitcoin. That model worked better when regulation was lighter, competition was lower, and unit economics were stronger. Over time, higher compliance costs and legal scrutiny started to erode that edge. Bitcoin Depot's filing shows how hard it is to keep that model profitable under the 2026 rule set.

**6. What are the short-term risks for investors?**

The main risk is contagion across other listed or privately held ATM operators if regulators keep tightening rules. Investors should also watch for distressed asset sales, further wallet security problems, and more lawsuits tied to compliance failures or consumer claims. Another risk is that market participants underestimate how quickly revenue can fall in this business. Once traffic and trust drop together, recovery gets much harder.
